nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae that bloom in the cold, nutrient-rich waters around the island and feed zooplankton and seafloor animals.

nodes.name: Bigelow's sedge
nodes.desc: A common tundra sedge. Sedges and grasses are the main summer forage for the island's grazing animals.

nodes.name: Arctic willows
nodes.desc: Dwarf willows such as grayleaf and creeping willow hug the ground. Muskoxen rely on willow most heavily in winter.

nodes.name: Tufted hairgrass
nodes.desc: A tussock grass of the island's warmer, drier valleys, where steppe-like meadows grow. Muskoxen prefer grasses when they are plentiful.

nodes.name: Arctic copepods
nodes.desc: Fat-rich zooplankton that graze the phytoplankton bloom and are eaten by Arctic cod and other small sea animals.

nodes.name: Seafloor clams
nodes.desc: Bottom-living clams and other bivalves. Pacific walruses prefer them, and benthic invertebrates make up most of the walrus diet.

nodes.name: Wrangel Island collared lemming
nodes.desc: The island has unusually dense lemming populations. Lemmings are the key prey of Arctic foxes, snowy owls and wolverines.

nodes.name: Snow goose
nodes.desc: The only snow goose population breeding in Asia, nesting in colonies on the island. Nests and goslings are exposed to foxes and jaegers.

nodes.name: Muskox
nodes.desc: Released onto the island in 1975 and now about a thousand strong. Eats grasses and willows; wolves are its main predator elsewhere.

nodes.name: Feral reindeer
nodes.desc: Domestic reindeer brought in during the 1950s now live wild, kept to about 1,000 animals to limit damage to bird nesting grounds.

nodes.name: Arctic cod
nodes.desc: A small cold-water fish that eats zooplankton and is a main food of ringed seals and many seabirds.

nodes.name: Ringed seal
nodes.desc: The seal most often taken by polar bears. Its pups wait in snow dens in spring, where Arctic foxes can also reach them.

nodes.name: Pacific walrus
nodes.desc: Wrangel hosts one of the largest walrus gatherings, up to 100,000 on one beach at a time. It dives for clams on the seafloor.

nodes.name: Arctic fox
nodes.desc: An omnivore for which lemmings are the most common prey. It also takes bird eggs, hunts seal pups and scavenges bear kills.

nodes.name: Snowy owl
nodes.desc: Breeds in high numbers only when lemmings are plentiful. On Wrangel it can find lemmings tunnelling under the snow by hearing them.

nodes.name: Parasitic jaeger
nodes.desc: A seabird of prey that nests on the tundra and takes lemmings and the eggs and chicks of other birds.

nodes.name: Wolverine
nodes.desc: A scavenger and predator that depends heavily on lemmings, and also feeds on carrion and larger animals.

nodes.name: Polar bear
nodes.desc: Wrangel has the densest known concentration of polar bear dens. Females den on the island while the bears hunt seals on the sea ice.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: The short, bright polar summer powers a brief burst of plant growth on land and plankton blooms at sea.

nodes.name: Cold, nutrient-rich water
nodes.desc: The surrounding seas are unusually rich in oxygen and nutrients, which supports plankton and the animals above them.

nodes.name: Sea ice
nodes.desc: Where algae grow beneath the ice and where polar bears hunt seals. Pack ice also shapes where walruses rest.

nodes.name: Tundra soil and permafrost
nodes.desc: Island ground that was never glaciated. Its thin, cold soil feeds sedges, willows and the meadows of the warmer valleys.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Microbes and fungi break down dead plants, droppings and carcasses slowly in the cold and return nutrients to the soil.
